# 13-aircaps: sources

Back-test entry `13-aircaps.yaml`. AirCaps, YC Fall 2025 (Launch YC 2025-11-05). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)
- **HT**: HearingTracker, "Hear with Your Eyes: A Review of Live Captioning Glasses". https://www.hearingtracker.com/hearing-glasses/hear-with-your-eyes-five-ar-live-captioning-glasses
- **DTS-ASL**: ASL Deafined blog, "Dinner Table Syndrome: What Deaf, DeafBlind, and Hard of Hearing People Face". https://blog.asldeafined.com/2025/05/dinner-table-syndrome-what-deaf-deafblind-and-hard-of-hearing-people-face/

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").
- Walter Nguyen: shortlist reading of SITE ("My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups") and the SITE family-conversation testimonial.
- Diego Herrera: SITE table-with-friends testimonial; DTS-ASL ("if others are facing away or talking too quickly, these visual cues can be lost").
- Amaka Obi: YC-L (phones break eye contact); SMI (phone subtitles leave users "stuck looking at their screens at all times"); SITE work testimonial.
- Ruth Feldman: SITE testimonial on "speeches and seminars in large spaces".
- Tomás Reyes: YALE, the first-year deaf in one ear with three friends in a café.
- Eleanor Park: YALE, the campus walk where construction noise nearly drowned the conversation.
- Colette Marchand: SITE testimonial on an uncaptioned movie theater; YALE screening.
- Andrea Whitlock: YALE, the Deaf ASL instructor who sees the glasses as one-directional and worries institutions could cut services. She is the sceptic who will not adopt.
- Gordon McBride: author's invention, filling a gap: a hearing-aid user whose quiet week went fine, the low-frequency case. It is the other side of SMI's "aren't dependable ... with a lot of background noise".
- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).
- Shirin Tehrani: SMI, the late-deafened user who relies "completely on live transcription and captions" and names doctor visits.
- Beatriz Souza: SMI ("Since the app needs the speaker to converse in English, I have not been able to use it much in social settings").
- Hollis Grant: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.
- Naomi Adler: author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story (rather not say). DTS-ASL on "frustration, anxiety, and even a reluctance to attend social events".
- Frank Dellinger: DTS-ASL (family dinners and gatherings, "talking over each other").
- Ingrid Solberg: author's invention, filling a gap: a counter conversation through a screen and a mask, where lipreading fails. DTS-ASL on lost visual cues.
- Patrick Moran: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No (a quiet week with no hard conversation).
- Lucia Ferraro: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.
- Desmond Hale: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

insights.line: What would make it clearly worth it?

whys.g1: The three answers are about different things (a trial matinee before ordering, picking up audience questions in a big hall, and a seating workaround), so none of them belongs in a group with another, and leaving each on its own is how I'd sort them too.
whys.g2: Tomás's answer describes his end-seat workaround rather than what would make the glasses worth it, so it's off the question, but it was left on its own and not grouped, and there is no other junk on the line.

founder.order_why: Mostly logical (context, problem, solution, launch), but the window question (screen 4) sits between two identical context screens, so the context step feels interrupted rather than finished before the problem starts.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 5 show the same kicker and the same question ('Before we test anything, let's define exactly where this idea applies.'); screen 4 also has typos ('aduts', 'hearingg').
founder.missing: Nothing about price or who pays: no screen asks what the glasses cost ($599, plus $20/month for Pro), what deaf and hard-of-hearing adults spend today on captioning apps or hearing-aid extras, or whether the wearer pays alone (HSA/FSA eligible). That leaves the commercial side of AirCaps untested.

PRIMARY.order_why: Screen 4 asks if I could read captions while watching faces before screen 6 tells me the captions are on glasses (and screen 5 calls AirCaps an app), so I answered 4 picturing a phone screen in my hand and would have answered differently knowing it was glasses.
PRIMARY.asked_twice: Screens 4 and 5 both send me back to a recent conversation and ask, in effect, whether captions would have helped; screen 2 already established I fell behind, so 4 and 5 feel like the same recall twice.
PRIMARY.missing: What I do now to keep up (lipreading, asking people to repeat, hearing aids or cochlear implant, a phone captioning app like Live Transcribe, an interpreter or CART), whether it was noise or speed or group talk that lost me, how often this happens in a week, and what I'd pay for glasses.

screens.instead: Which one do you want to test? -- Could read captions while watching faces (suggested: the habit lipreaders lean on most) · Had their phone online; bar: holds if no more than 1 in 3 say only sometimes or no.

screens.why1: Once compatibility is settled, the next obvious question is what the glasses do better than phone captions, hearing aids or nodding along.
screens.why2: The question is plain to me as a founder, though the hint's example 'less time on it each week' is a chore-tool benefit, not a conversation one, so it gives me little to go on.
screens.why3: I know from testimonials and our co-founder's own experience exactly what people get that today's way doesn't give them.
screens.why4: It is a box for up to four rows with 'I'm not sure' as the only chip, which fits a founder who can't name a benefit; my one row fits in nine words.
screens.why5: My typed benefit, 'More of the talk followed without asking for repeats', is kept as I wrote it and is still what I mean.
screens.why7: The box asks for 1 to 4 benefits of at most 9 words each, compared with today's way, with 'I'm not sure' as the escape, and my single noun-phrase row meets that shape; leaving out eye contact versus a phone screen is my choice, not a fault of the screen.
screens.instead: Same question, with a hint example from conversation, e.g. "eyes kept on faces, not on a phone".

screens.why1: Right after I typed what AirCaps does better than today's way, it's obvious Keel shows back the benefit it will test before I move on to the price side.
screens.why2: I'd say 'following more of the conversation without asking people to repeat', and 'more of the talk followed' is stilted; in the belief, 'would have given them more of the talk followed' needs a second read.
screens.why3: Losing the thread at a table with hearing people and having to ask for repeats is exactly what my wearers and I know first-hand.
screens.why4: One clean row at the 9-word cap, under the 1-to-4 guidance; nothing is missing, because this is the one gain I lead with.
screens.why5: It still means my 'Following more without asking anyone to repeat': same gain, only the word order is changed.
screens.why7: Today's top rung 'Followed everything that was said' doesn't already give it; it's one gain on one row; and the belief carries it against the hard case as one moment that went wrong, 'the last time they lost the conversation with hearing people', not any occasion.
screens.instead: Row: 'Following more of the talk without asking for repeats'; belief: '...the last time they lost the conversation with hearing people, they would have followed more of it without asking for repeats.'

screens.why1: After what it fits into and what it does better, asking what my wearers have to do to start is the obvious next question about the idea, and nothing earlier asked it.
screens.why2: 'What will they have to do to start using it?' with 'setup, extra steps or learning' is plain to me, and I answered it straight away in my own words.
screens.why3: I know exactly what a wearer takes on: putting the glasses on in the conversations that matter and keeping them charged, which our power users do every day.
screens.why4: This is a box to type into with up to four rows; 'I'm not sure' is the right way out on the founder's side, and my two rows are distinct.
screens.why5: My two efforts sit there as I typed them, wearing the glasses in conversations and charging them daily, with no rewording yet.
screens.why7: Both rows are efforts the wearer takes themselves, short base-form verb phrases in one voice; the daily charge is the new habit the card wants, and neither repeats Compatibility's phone-online row.

screens.why1: Right after I said what they have to do to start, Keel shows the efforts back for me to check, so it is obvious why it is asked here.
screens.why2: Wearing the caption glasses and charging them every day are my words and my wearers' words; only the intro repeating its own title reads a little clumsily.
screens.why3: Whether they would wear the glasses at the table and charge them each night is exactly what a deaf or hard-of-hearing adult knows about their own week.
screens.why4: The two rows are distinct and in plain words, but the one-time setup my glasses actually need, pairing them to the phone app, is missing as a row or a suggestion.
screens.why5: Wear the caption glasses in conversations is my revision-24 wording kept, and daily charging is a true cost of my device; nothing drifted.
screens.why7: Each row is one effort of under 9 words, a base-form verb phrase the wearer takes themselves, in one voice, with no sign-off or Compatibility condition, and either could be supported or refuted on the fixed four plus I can't tell.
screens.instead: Rows: Wear the caption glasses in conversations · Charge the glasses every day · Pair the glasses with the app on their phone (Keel's suggestion: the one-time setup before first use).

screens.why1: Right after I said what it takes to start, Keel asks which effort is most likely to stop people, which is the obvious next question before it tests one.
screens.why2: 'Wear the caption glasses in conversations' and 'Charge the glasses every day' are how I talk about the product, and I can answer them on first reading.
screens.why3: I know from our power users and returns which of these trips people up: putting visible glasses on at a table is the real hurdle, and daily charging is a smaller one.
screens.why4: Two distinct efforts the wearer takes themselves, in my words, with no overlap and nothing nonsensical; the phone-online step stays where it belongs, on Compatibility.
screens.why5: My 'wear the glasses' effort is kept as I revised it, and the pairing part now lives on the Compatibility screen, so nothing I meant is lost.
screens.why7: Both rows are one effort each, base-form, in the wearer's voice and taken by the wearer, none repeats Compatibility or Purchase friction, and the belief 'Most would wear the caption glasses in conversations' can be supported or refuted by Yes / Only if / Probably not / No, with I can't tell as the escape.

screens.why1: Asking whether to collect emails from people who'd try it for real fits right before the study goes out, and as AirCaps with 15-day free returns I want those leads.
screens.why2: Pilot, email and yes/no are plain to a founder, and the hint says exactly what the respondent will see.
screens.why3: Whether I want buyers to raise their hand is my own call, answerable at once.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers it, the two options are distinct, and no escape is needed for a founder's own decision.
screens.why5: The meaning is kept, but 'try this for real' is vague for glasses someone has to order and wear, and doesn't hint at the order-with-free-returns step I typed as the commitment.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? Hint: people who say yes see "Would you try the caption glasses for real, with free returns? Leave your email." (Yes, ask them / No pilot)

screens.why1: Picking the interviewer belongs just before launch, but asking me to choose a voice for deaf and hard-of-hearing people feels abrupt unless the screen first settles how they will take the questions in.
screens.why2: Two names, a 5-second preview and a credit cost are plain to me on first reading, and the hint says outright that every question is also written and can be answered by typing or tapping.
screens.why3: I can judge a voice, but many of my respondents won't hear it, and what matters to them is whether the face lipreads well and the text shows clearly, which a 5-second audio clip doesn't let me judge.
screens.why4: Daphne and Saskia are distinct, but for my audience the missing option is a text-first or captions-only interviewer with no voice chosen, and that is the one many of them would want.
screens.why5: It keeps my people as 'deaf or hard-of-hearing adults' and leaks nothing of the glasses or roles to respondents.
screens.instead: How should the questions reach deaf or hard-of-hearing adults? Written on screen with a captioned video interviewer (Daphne ▶ / Saskia ▶, preview shows face and captions) · Written on screen only, no voice

screens.why1: Choosing how the study reaches my respondents is the natural last step after picking who asks the questions, just before sending.
screens.why2: The three choices are short and plain, and 'Read and tap' says exactly what my deaf and hard-of-hearing respondents would do.
screens.why3: I know my people: many prefer text to audio, so this is a call I can make from what I see every day.
screens.why4: The options are complete and distinct, but Daphne's description opens with 'asks each question aloud' for an audience that largely can't hear; the written-on-screen part, the part that matters to them, comes second.
screens.why5: My answer 'Read and tap' stands as picked, and nothing of AirCaps leaks into how the study is delivered.
screens.instead: How should deaf or hard-of-hearing adults answer? -- Read and tap (questions in text, answer by tapping or typing) / AI interviewer Daphne (every question written on screen, also spoken aloud on video) / Let them choose

screens.why1: Once I've picked how deaf and hard-of-hearing adults will answer, the obvious next step is deciding who receives the link, so this belongs at the end of the flow.
screens.why2: As a founder already inside Keel, 'link', 'Contacts page' and 'signs in with Google' read plainly on first pass, and each option says in a line what happens.
screens.why3: I know whether I'm sending to people I know, like hard-of-hearing users and family testimonials, or posting into a community like an HLAA chapter or a Deaf/HoH Facebook group, so this is answerable from my own work.
screens.why4: The three routes (named people, a Keel-found list, one open link in a group) are distinct and cover how I'd actually reach people, and no escape is needed for a routing choice.
screens.why5: My pick, people I know by name each getting their own link, is kept exactly, and nothing about AirCaps or the wearer role leaks to respondents.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits under the title with "3 beliefs: 3 holding", and each card shows 7 of 7 against a bar of 5 of 7, so I can see why it held.
screens.why_b2: There is no chart on this page, but each card line says what was counted (said yes / would have gone better / would do it), over 7 people, and where the bar sits (5 of 7), so I read it at a glance.
screens.why_b3: The card beliefs are recognisably mine, but the statement under the title is broken: it says "the deaf or hard-of-hearing adult wearing the glasses the app on the lightweight glasses shows live captions" and then repeats "gets back live captions", and the relative-advantage line is a clumsy splice of my words.
screens.why_b4: Nothing says what to do next; "What it measures" explains the method, and nothing tells me whether to move to pricing, or to follow up on the 3 who would only wear the glasses on a condition.
screens.why_b5: n=7 is visible, but a unanimous 7 of 7 from seven people is presented as plainly holding without saying it is a small sample, and the 3 conditional wearers are folded into the count as a quiet footnote.
screens.instead: Holding up on all three, from 7 people (a small group): all 7 could read captions while watching faces and all 7 said they would have followed a lot more; 3 of the 7 would only wear the glasses on a condition, so read those conditions before you price.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 7 of 7 against my bar of 5 of 7, so I know it held and which number decided it.
screens.why_b2: Four bars of yes/no answers over 7 people, all seven cells in the strip for me, and the marker at 5. What is counted, the n and the bar are plain at a glance.
screens.why_b3: Compatibility and 'could read captions while watching faces' are the condition I picked on the way in, in my words.
screens.why_b4: It tells me that reading captions while watching faces is not where AirCaps will fail, and points me to adoption friction as the thing to look at next.
screens.why_b5: The count line honestly calls 7 people a lean, not a call, but the So line flatly says this 'is not what will stop them' and that adoption friction 'is', which is firmer than seven answers can carry.
screens.instead: Among these 7, reading captions while watching faces looks unlikely to be what stops them; check adoption friction, below, next.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 7 of 7 against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know it held and which number decided it.
screens.why_b2: The bar and the 7 people are plain, but 'Better · 7 7 a lot · 0 a little' repeats the 7 and takes a second look to see that all seven are 'a lot'.
screens.why_b3: The belief line carries my benefit and my circumstance, but the question calls AirCaps 'an app' when what I sell is caption glasses, so the thing they judged is not quite mine.
screens.why_b4: It says all 7 imagined it going better and sends me to Adoption friction for whether they would actually wear the glasses, which is the real open question for me.
screens.why_b5: It keeps n visible and says 'a lean, not a call', but the people were asked about 'an app', so 7 of 7 'a lot better' may be about phone captions they already have, not my glasses.
screens.instead: Ask about 'AirCaps, caption glasses' rather than 'an app', and draw the bar as '7 better (7 a lot, 0 a little)'.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 7 of 7 would do it against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know it held and which number decided it.
screens.why_b2: Four bars of answers over 7 people, all 7 cells for me, and the marker at 5 are plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: Adoption friction and 'Most would wear the caption glasses in conversations' are my words; the asked line drops 'caption', but it is still my clause.
screens.why_b4: The So line only points below, and of the three notes just one is a concrete next step (Harriet's loaner for a matinee, which tells me to push the 15-day free returns harder), Ruth's is a feature ask and Tomás's is his own workaround, so I have to work out the action myself.
screens.why_b5: The small group is flagged as a lean, not a call, but 'what would make it worth it to those 3 is below' overclaims: Tomás's note is his end-seat workaround, not a condition, and 'fits into how I talk' is too vague to tell me what the catch really is.
screens.instead: 7 of 7 would wear them, 3 on a condition, a lean from 7 people; Harriet wants to try a pair at a matinee first, so lead with the 15-day free returns, and Ruth needs audience questions picked up in big halls.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'held' sits beside its number, 7 of 7 would do it against a bar of 5 of 7, both in the status line and again above the quotes.
screens.why_b3: Adoption friction and 'Most would wear the caption glasses in conversations' are the dimension and the belief I checked, worded as revision 25 left them.
screens.why_b4: 'Adoption friction held, 7 of 7; what they added' is a generic line; it does not say what to do, such as pointing Harriet's borrow-first ask at our 15-day returns or treating Ruth's audience-questions ask as a microphone-range gap to test.
screens.why_b5: It says 'held, 7 of 7' without saying 3 of those 7 yeses carry a condition, so the clean 7 of 7 is a soft overstatement; Tomás's quote even says his end-seat workaround 'works most of the time', which reads more like a reason not to buy than a condition to buy, and the small n of 7 is never flagged.
screens.why_b6: Three things I did not type: one-sided hearing loss already has a cheap seating workaround, the lens may be hard to read under stage lights, and in large halls the value lies in picking up audience questions, not just the speaker; the dangling 'Only if it fits into how I talk for' labels are noise around them.
screens.instead: Held, 7 of 7 (bar 5 of 7), but 3 of the yeses are conditional: Harriet wants a trial under stage lights, so point her to the 15-day returns; Ruth needs audience questions picked up in big halls, so test the mic range; and Tomás's end-seat trick already works for him, so one-sided loss may be a weak wedge.

screens.why1: A first screen that checks I talk with hearing people at all makes sense before asking me about following those conversations.
screens.why2: Short and in my own words; I know straight away whether I talk with hearing people each week.
screens.why3: It's about my own week at work, at the shops and with family, which I know without guessing.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, don't overlap, and a gate needs no escape.
screens.why5: Nothing of the product leaks, but it drops the face-to-face part and asks about a habit, not the last 7 days, so it would count me on text or email chats too.
screens.why6: Easy to hear and answer, but 'I'll read 2 options' before a plain yes-or-no is clunky where the guidelines say just 'Yes or no.'
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did you talk face to face with a hearing person? Yes or no.

screens.why1: Right after asking whether I talk with hearing people every week, it makes sense to ask whether I lost track in one of those conversations this past week before asking for the story.
screens.why2: Falling behind in a conversation is exactly what happens to me, and I'd say it the same way or as 'lost track', so I can answer it on first hearing.
screens.why3: I know exactly whether I lost the thread at dinner, at work or at the counter this week, so I can answer it from my own life.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it with no overlap, and the chips beside it belong to the story box after a Yes, not to this question.
screens.why5: It names the trouble I actually have, without any product, company idea or label for people like me that I wouldn't use.
screens.why6: It's one short question with Yes or no at the end, easy to catch in one hearing, and better still with captions on screen.
screens.why7: The gate names the window and the costly moment, falling behind, rather than the routine of talking with hearing people, so someone who kept up in a quiet one-on-one can truly say No, and the bare Yes or No has no escape, as the card requires.

screens.why1: After asking whether I fell behind in a conversation this week, it makes sense to show me the idea before asking what I think of it.
screens.why2: Live captions, glasses and eye contact are everyday words to me; I use captions all the time and I know what losing eye contact costs when I look down at a phone.
screens.why3: It describes my own situation: people talking around me and me trying to read words without losing their faces.
screens.why4: A card to read with no options.
screens.why5: This is a deliberate idea card that names the product and what it does in plain terms, and nothing in it leaks the founder's labels for me.
screens.why6: Three short sentences with no symbols or brackets, and AirCaps is easy to say; on the phone I would follow it the way I follow any caption.

screens.why1: Right after the glasses idea, the obvious next question is whether I could actually take in captions and still watch people's faces, since lipreading and expressions are half of how I follow.
screens.why2: "Read captions while watching faces" is how I'd put it, but "your last conversation" doesn't say with hearing people, and my last one might have been signing with a deaf friend, where captions mean nothing.
screens.why3: I read captions on TV and on Live Transcribe while glancing up at people, so I know from my own life whether I can do both at once, even though I had no glasses that day.
screens.why4: Easily, most of the time, sometimes, and no are the real answers for juggling text and faces, and "I can't tell" fits someone who has never tried captions live.
screens.why5: The product only shows on the idea card, as intended, and the question itself uses my words, not a company's.
screens.why6: One short question and four short options; I could hold it after hearing it once (or reading it, since I wouldn't be hearing it).
screens.why7: This is an ability row with the ability four in order, two for and two against, and the one escape set apart; it tests the step the idea rests on (eyes on text and faces together), which some of us can do and some can't, so it can go either way.
screens.instead: Think of your last conversation with hearing people. Could you have read captions while watching their faces? Yes, easily · Yes, most of the time · Only sometimes · No · I can't tell

screens.why1: Right after the idea card and the captions-while-watching-faces question, asking whether it would have helped the last time I lost the thread is the obvious next thing.
screens.why2: I know straight away what losing the conversation means, but 'follow and join' is two things in one breath: captions would help me follow, while joining in is a different matter, and I would pause over which one I'm judging.
screens.why3: I can name the last time I lost the thread with hearing people this week, and I can picture whether captions on glasses would have changed it.
screens.why4: A lot better, a little better, no difference and worse cover it cleanly, and 'I can't tell' fits someone who has never worn caption glasses.
screens.why5: It names AirCaps as the card showed it and asks only about my conversation, with none of the founder's benefits pushed at me.
screens.why6: Heard once it holds together: one moment, one question, four short options I can keep in my head, then the escape.
screens.why7: The anchor is the moment it went wrong rather than any conversation, the fixed four sit in order with No difference and Worse on the scale, no benefit is named, and 'I can't tell' is the one escape, so the belief can be both supported and refuted.
screens.instead: Think of the most recent time you lost the conversation with hearing people. Would AirCaps have helped you keep up with it better, or not? A lot better · A little better · No difference · Worse · I can't tell

screens.why1: After the idea and whether it would have helped, asking whether I'd actually put the glasses on in my conversations is the obvious next thing to ask.
screens.why2: Wear the glasses in your conversations is plain to me, and I can answer it on first reading.
screens.why3: I know whether I'd wear captioning glasses with hearing people at work, at the shop, with family, so I can answer from my own life.
screens.why4: The four are distinct and complete, but 'only if it fits into how I talk' is vague to me; my real condition would be about whether it keeps up, or whether people stare at the glasses or think I'm recording them.
screens.why5: The idea card names the product on purpose and nothing else of the founder's plan or terms reaches me.
screens.why6: Short, one question, four short options and one escape, easy to hold when heard once.
screens.why7: Wearing the glasses is my own new habit and the scale, balance and escape all follow the card, but the 'Only if' condition is close to true of any step rather than naming the assurance that would make me say yes.
screens.instead: To use AirCaps, you'd wear the glasses in your conversations. Would you do that, or not? Yes · Only if the captions kept up · Probably not · No · I can't tell

screens.why1: After being asked whether I'd wear the glasses, asking what would make it worth it is a natural last question before I go.
screens.why2: Short and plain; I can answer it on first reading, and it names AirCaps instead of a bare 'it'.
screens.why3: I know what I'd need: captions that keep up in a noisy restaurant and let me keep my eyes on faces, so I can answer from my own life.
screens.why4: A box to type in, with no options.
screens.why5: AirCaps was named on the idea card, and nothing new about the founder's plan or their words for people reaches me here.
screens.why6: One short question, easy to hear once and answer out loud.

typo_leaks.text: How far back should deaf or hard-of-hearing aduts look for the last time a conversation with hearingg people is too fast or too noisy to follow?
